“Submitted, rejected; rejected, resubmitted; resubmitted, rejected again. Tempered a thousand times. Still not happy? Quit the game and stay safe.” — Zhao Benshan, Northeast China’s king of comedy sketches

I once submitted to journal A, a so-called top journal in my field (impact factor under 2, facepalm), and it ended in tragedy after a savaging from the eternal villain, Reviewer 2. I then sent it to journal B, a notch below, and got in, except that by the time it was accepted, I had already quit research to stay safe. Rejection is perfectly normal, really. Steph Curry is deadly from deep, but does every one of his threes go in? His percentage isn’t even over 50%, is it? But even though it’s normal, and you’re supposed to take it in stride, actually seeing that rejection still makes you clench up and feel that fate is against you. Funnily enough, the reviewer who rejected me and the reviewer who accepted me came to almost completely opposite conclusions, which left me not knowing whether to laugh or cry. That’s the mystery of publishing. Your fate rests in the hands of at most 3.5 people: ≤3 reviewers plus 1 editor, who counts as half a reviewer. I’m no great researcher myself and never expected to make a name in academia, but after writing a few papers I did get a feel for the writing. To put it more bluntly: I know how to talk, how to chat with reviewers. More bluntly still: how to package your work, even when it isn’t perfect (just don’t let the reviewer notice). And most bluntly of all: even if it’s crap, don’t let anyone smell it. Just my two cents; the big shots can skip this.

My experience with journal A:

First round: major revision. R1 was neutral, leaning positive. R2 said this:

No novelty: that’s basically a wholesale rejection. R2 raised a whole pile of issues. I spent ages writing a rebuttal letter, and then he or she said this:

Still not convinced. To finish me off for good, R2 dug up a heap of unrelated literature to prove that I really had no novelty and hadn’t even got the most basic literature review right. With those two blows together, the paper was basically on death row, and it was duly rejected. When the rejection letter came, I was sitting outside the Centre Pompidou with a childhood friend, and my mood sank on the spot. But I got over it soon enough, bought a load of groceries and went home to cook. Why? Maybe I already knew I wouldn’t stay in research, so I didn’t care that much, haha.

That said, even though R2 was a real bitch, my writing really did have problems. R1 raised similar issues: they couldn’t tell what I was actually trying to do. Looking back on my state of mind then, I was trying to cover too much, so I inevitably lost sight of some things, stressing this and that until readers came away with no idea what it was all about. Apart from that, the overall writing was fine; the two esteemed reviewers didn’t say much about it.

By the time I regrouped and submitted to the next journal, almost half a year had passed. In between I defended my PhD, traveled with my parents, quit my university job and looked for work, and had neither the time nor the heart to deal with it. This time I learned my lesson: one goal, just explain one thing clearly. I cut a lot of hot air that had nothing to do with the topic and focused on telling one story well, and the first round of reviews was fairly positive.

This time was the exception: R2 raised a dozen or so minor points, sorted in minutes. R1 first acknowledged the significance of my work, then said my writing wasn’t up to scratch. I laughed when I read it: partly because it looked very promising, and partly because, damn, this was almost the exact opposite of what the earlier R2 had said (about the research itself)! And the writing problems they picked on weren’t even of the same kind. So I became even more convinced: whether a paper is rejected or accepted depends far too much on the reviewers’ field and competence. Clearly neither the earlier R2 nor this R1 worked in my area, because however unclear the writing, someone from the same area wouldn’t have raised those questions. And a less competent reviewer offers minor comments when in a good mood and opens fire on you when in a bad one. There are a thousand reasons to reject a paper; pick a few in any combination, and months or even years of hard work get shot down. If that 0.5 reviewer, the editor, is conscientious and understands your work reasonably well, they might give you another chance, even if the reviewer is a bitch. But how many editors like that are there? So my conclusion: when it comes to publishing, doesn’t luck play a bit too big a part?

Of course, we’re young; get rejected once and you can try again. With enough grinding, even an iron rod becomes a needle, and even a paper gets accepted. But shouldn’t we think about the time and energy that goes into it? If the experiments, simulations and theory are all in place, is all that’s left just rewriting it every which way to please the reviewers? Take me: from submitting to journal A to journal B accepting it a few days ago took a full year and a half. Leave out the half year when I wasn’t touching the paper, and it’s still a whole year (including time spent waiting for decisions). And I’m counting from submission. What about the time before that? One of my master’s students worked on it for over half a year, and I spent nearly two months writing it. Of course the preparatory work is necessary; whether or not you’re in academia, that kind of work has to be done. But in the year that followed, although I wasn’t working on the paper every day, the time I did spend on it was nothing but word games. Maybe a few new figures, a few simulations redone, but the main work had long been finished.

You play word games for ages, and then the power of life and death rests with at most 3.5 people. Isn’t that game a bit unfair?

In academia I’ve seen two kinds of people. One is the publication machine: academically top-notch, writing down to a formula, turning out a paper in a week, no problem. They get endless pleasure from years of fighting with reviewers, and the fun goes up a level when they review other people’s papers. To me, these people were born for academia and can go far. The other kind, the majority, find writing papers painful; academia is just a way to make a living. Only when a paper is accepted do they feel some consolation; then they numb themselves, tell themselves that research is actually fun and rewarding, and go on squeezing out the next paper.

So, after all that: what’s it like to have an SCI paper rejected? It hurts, of course! But if you find that rejection isn’t the only part of academic life that makes you miserable, then squeeze out enough papers to get your PhD and get out of academia as early as you can!
